title: Riesz Representation of Positive Linear Functionals
preview: Recall that a measure space consists of three basic components: a set X ; a σ -algebra M on X ; a (positive, or unsigned) measure μ : M → [ 0 , + ∞ ] . If X is a topological space , then there is another way than outer measures to construct measurable sets and measures, namely via the celebrated Riesz representation theorem .

With a topology on X and some extra assumptions on it, one can start with evaluating integrals of continuous functions over compact sets using piecewise constant functions , i.e. Riemann integration. This first contruction is more natural as for the topological space X , in the sense that one does NOT need extra data, compared to evaluating integrals using simple finctions, presuming the construction of measurable sets on X .

It is of interest to ask whether one can complete this "Riemann model'' to the "Lebesgue model'' in a standard way; the answer is affirmative, given by the Riesz representation, and even more is true.

Recall that a measure space consists of three basic components: a set X {X}X; a σ {\sigma}σ-algebra M {\mathfrak{M}}M on X {X}X; a (positive, or unsigned) measure μ:M→[0,+∞] {\mu:\mathfrak{M}\rightarrow[0,+\infty]}μ:M→[0,+∞]. If X {X}X is a topological space, then there is another way than outer measures to construct measurable sets and measures, namely via the celebrated Riesz representation theorem.

With a topology on X {X}X and some extra assumptions on it, one can start with evaluating integrals of continuous functions over compact sets using piecewise constant functions, i.e. Riemann integration. This first contruction is more natural as for the topological space X {X}X, in the sense that one does NOT need extra data, compared to evaluating integrals using simple finctions, presuming the construction of measurable sets on X {X}X.

It is of interest to ask whether one can complete this "Riemann model'' to the "Lebesgue model'' in a standard way; the answer is affirmative, given by the Riesz representation, and even more is true.

Taking a slight abstraction, the data of the "Riemann model'' can be thought of as a positive linear functional as follows. Denote by Cc(X)=Cc(X→R) {C_{c}(X)=C_{c}(X\rightarrow\mathbb{R})}Cc​(X)=Cc​(X→R) to be the space of real-valued continuous functions with compact support in X {X}X. A linear functional Λ:Cc(X)→R {\Lambda:C_{c}(X)\rightarrow\mathbb{\mathbb{R}}}Λ:Cc​(X)→R is said to be positive if

Λf≥0 whenever f≥0.\displaystyle \Lambda f\geq0\text{ whenever }f\geq0.Λf≥0 whenever f≥0.

Given any open subset G⊂X {G\subset X}G⊂X, consider the class of continuous functions f {f}f such that 0≤f≤1 {0\leq f\leq1}0≤f≤1 on G {G}G and f=0 {f=0}f=0 outside of G {G}G, denoted by f≺G {f\prec G}f≺G. To get some idea, we can first define the "measure'' of the set G {G}G by

μ(G)=sup⁡f≺GΛf.\displaystyle \mu(G)=\sup_{f\prec G}\Lambda f. μ(G)=f≺Gsup​Λf.

In fact, one can use open sets as a gauge to construct an outer measure using the above definition. The Riesz representation theorem says that there corresponds a unique unsigned Borel measure that "does the same thing'' with the linear functional. Notice that an unsigned Borel measure can be obviously ensembled to be a linear functional.

However, it is rather intricate to find the right condition for the sets to be measurable (in the sense of Caratheodory). The main techinical issue in developing this machinary is, not surprisingly, topological.

In the following, I shall follow both of the Rudin's book [R] and Terry's notes.

**

1. Urysohn's lemma

**

Let X {X}X be a topological space. It is not always possible to approximate the indicator function of a closed set using continuous functions in a reasonable way. However, we do have a characterization of when it is possible.

Lemma 1 (Urysohn) The following are equivalent:

*- Every pair of disjoint closed sets F1,F2 {F_{1},F_{2}}F1​,F2​ in X {X}X can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods G1⊃F1 {G_{1}\supset F_{1}}G1​⊃F1​, G2⊃F2 {G_{2}\supset F_{2}}G2​⊃F2​.

  • For every closed set F {F}F in X {X}X and every open neighborhood G {G}G of F {F}F, there exists a continuous function f:X→[0,1] {f:X\rightarrow[0,1]}f:X→[0,1] such that

    χF(x)≤f(x)≤χG(x),\displaystyle \chi_{F}(x)\leq f(x)\leq\chi_{G}(x),χF​(x)≤f(x)≤χG​(x),

    for which we will also write F≺f≺G {F\prec f\prec G}F≺f≺G.*

A topological space satisfying one of the above properties is said to be normal.
Proof: Assume the first statement. By noticing that the complement of open set is closed, it is equivalent to the statement for every closed set F1 {{F_{1}}}F1​ in X {X}X and every open neighborhood G0 {G_{0}}G0​ of F1 {F_{1}}F1​, there exists an open set G1/2 {G_{1/2}}G1/2​ and a closed set F1/2 {F_{1/2}}F1/2​ such that

F1⊂G1/2⊂F1/2⊂G0.\displaystyle F_{1}\subset G_{1/2}\subset F_{1/2}\subset G_{0}.F1​⊂G1/2​⊂F1/2​⊂G0​.

Since dyadic rationals are dense in [0,1] {[0,1]}[0,1], we have for a∈[0,1] {a\in[0,1]}a∈[0,1], sets such as

are open, and consequently f {f}f is continuous. Conversely, the second statement is equivalent to that for every pair of disjoint closed sets F1,F2 {F_{1},F_{2}}F1​,F2​, there is a continuous function f:X→[0,1] {f:X\rightarrow[0,1]}f:X→[0,1] such that f=1 {f=1}f=1 on F1 {F_{1}}F1​ and f=0 {f=0}f=0 on F2 {F_{2}}F2​. Then the sets f−1(x>2/3) {f^{-1}(x>2/3)}f−1(x>2/3) and f−1(x<1/3) {f^{-1}(x<1/3)}f−1(x<1/3) are open and disjoint, and containing F1 {F_{1}}F1​ and F2 {F_{2}}F2​ respectively.□ \Box□

Remark 1 A topological space X {X}X being normal is a separation property, viz. the ability to distinguish distinct sets via topological methods. It turns out that the study of separation properties is a quite delicate matter. For instance, listed in an order of increasing strength, two subsets A,B {A,B}A,B are said to be separated if each is disjoint from the other's closure; to be separated by neighborhoods if they have disjoint neighborhoods; to be separated by closed neighborhoods; to be separated by continuous function if there exists a continuous function from X {X}X to R {\mathbb{R}}R taking distinct constant values on each set; to be precisely separated by continuous functions if there exists a continuous function with each pre-image of two distinct singleton being exactly each set respectively. Urysohn's lemma thus establishes the equivalence between the separation of closed sets by neighborhoods and by continuous functions.

A topological space is said to be Hausdorff if two distinct points can be separated by neighborhoods. Clearly, if X {X}X is normal and every point in it is closed, then X {X}X is also Hausdorff. Unfortunately, the converse it not true. However, for compact ones we do have:

Lemma 2 A compact Hausdorff space is normal.

The Hausdorff property can well be extended to subspaces of a Hausdorff space, while the normal property CANNOT.

Now back to the "Riemann model''. Besides separation property, as in integration on Rn {\mathbb{R}^{n}}Rn we would also require some local "smallness'' for the space, so that the integration makes sense at least locally. A property in this respect is locally compactness. Now we have our model space of study.

Definition 3 A topological space X {X}X is said to be locally compact Hausdorff, abbr. LCH, if X {X}X is Hausdorff, and every point in X {X}X has a neighborhood with compact closure, i.e. a relatively compact neighborhood.

In light of Lemma 2, one can establish a Urysohn type of result for LCH spaces.

Lemma 4 (Urysohn's lemma)Let X {X}X be a LCH space, K⊂X {K\subset X}K⊂X a compact subset, and G {G}G be a open neighborhood of K {K}K. Then there exists a function f∈Cc(X) {f\in C_{c}(X)}f∈Cc​(X) such that K≺f≺G {K\prec f\prec G}K≺f≺G.

Proof: Let Ux {U_{x}}Ux​ be a open neighborhood of x {x}x with compact closure. Then the collection {Ux}x∈K {\{U_{x}\}_{x\in K}}{Ux​}x∈K​ forms an open cover of K {K}K. Since K {K}K is compact, there exists a finite subfamily {U1,…,UN} {\{U_{1},\dots,U_{N}\}}{U1​,…,UN​} that forms a cover of K {K}K, whose union has compact closure. Let G′=⋃n=1NUn∩G {G'=\bigcup_{n=1}^{N}U_{n}\cap G}G′=⋃n=1N​Un​∩G. Then G′‾ {\overline{G'}}G′ is a compact Hausdorff space. Now apply Lemma 2 to get a continuous function f {f}f on G′‾ {\overline{G'}}G′, and define f=0 {f=0}f=0 outside of G′‾ {\overline{G'}}G′. □ \Box□

Here we see that LCH spaces are desirable for approximation using functions in Cc(X) {C_{c}(X)}Cc​(X).

Sometimes it is convenient to have spaces that allows us to extend local construction globally, using partition of unity. The property we need in addition is that the open cover {Uα}α∈A {\{U_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in A}}{Uα​}α∈A​ is finitely overlapping, meaning that every x∈X {x\in X}x∈X belongs to at most finitely many Uα {U_{\alpha}}Uα​. Topological spaces that have for every open cover a finitely overlapping refinement will be called paracompact. The construction of partition of unity follows straightforwardly from Lemma 4.

2. the Riesz representation theorem and regularity of Borel measures

Now we are ready to build up the machinery that completes the "Riemann model'' to the "Lebesgue model'' on a LCH space X {X}X. The "Lebesgue model'' here refers to a measure space (X,M,μ) {(X,\mathfrak{M},\mu)}(X,M,μ) such that μ {\mu}μ restricts to a Borel measure. Recall that the Borel σ {\sigma}σ-algebra on X {X}X is the smallest σ {\sigma}σ-algebra on X {X}X that contains all the open sets in X {X}X.

Definition 6 (Unsigned Borel Measure) Let X {X}X be a LCH space. A measure μ:B→[0,+∞] {\mu:\mathcal{B}\rightarrow[0,+\infty]}μ:B→[0,+∞] is called Borel if B {\mathcal{B}}B is the Borel σ {\sigma}σ-algebra on X {X}X.

As we will see later, X {X}X being merely LCH will give rise to some regularity issues of the constructed Borel measure. So addtionally we need assume X {X}X to be σ {\sigma}σ-compact so that these regularity issues disappear. It is thus useful to have the following definiton:

Definition 7 (Unsigned Radon Measure, regularity) Let X {X}X be a LCH space that is also σ {\sigma}σ-compact, and let B {\mathcal{B}}B be the Borel σ {\sigma}σ-algebra. An unisigned Radon measure is a unsigned Borel measure μ:B→[0,+∞] {\mu:\mathcal{B}\rightarrow[0,+\infty]}μ:B→[0,+∞] with the following regularity properties:

*- (Local finiteness) For any compact subset K {K}K of X {X}X, μ(K) {\mu(K)}μ(K) is finte;

  • (Outer regularity) For any Borel set E∈B {E\in\mathcal{B}}E∈B , μ(E)=inf⁡{μ(G):G⊃E, and G open} {\mu(E)=\inf\{\mu(G):G\supset E,\text{ and }G\text{ open}\}}μ(E)=inf{μ(G):G⊃E, and G open};
  • (Inner regularity) For any Borel set E∈B {E\in\mathcal{B}}E∈B, μ(E)=sup⁡{μ(K):K⊂E, and K compact} {\mu(E)=\sup\{\mu(K):K\subset E,\text{ and }K\text{ compact}\}}μ(E)=sup{μ(K):K⊂E, and K compact}.*

Remark 2 Note that in the construction of outer measures, outer regularity is built-in for any set. There also exist constructions of Radon measures on spaces that are not σ\sigmaσ-compact or not LCH, but we will not touch this point.

Now we start our construction. Given a positive linear functional Λ:Cc(X)→R {\Lambda:C_{c}(X)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}}Λ:Cc​(X)→R, for every open set G⊂X {G\subset X}G⊂X, we define as in (⋆\star⋆):

μ(G)=sup⁡f≺GΛf.(2) \displaystyle \mu(G)=\sup_{f\prec G}\Lambda f. (2)μ(G)=f≺Gsup​Λf.(2)

μ(E)=inf⁡{μ(G):G⊃E, and G open}.(3) \displaystyle \mu(E)=\inf\{\mu(G):G\supset E,\text{ and }G\text{ open}\}. (3)μ(E)=inf{μ(G):G⊃E, and G open}.(3)

As Caratheodory's measurability suggests, we need sets that can be "approximated from below'', i.e. those inner regular ones to form a σ {\sigma}σ-algebra and thus a measure space. Then by Caratheodory's extension theorem, the measure space will be complete. So define

Mc={E⊂X:μ(E)<+∞ and E is inner regular},\displaystyle \mathfrak{M}_{c}=\{E\subset X:\mu(E)<+\infty\text{ and }E\text{ is inner regular}\},Mc​={E⊂X:μ(E)<+∞ and E is inner regular},

Λf=∫Xfdμ.(5) \displaystyle \Lambda f=\int_{X}fd\mu. (5)Λf=∫X​fdμ.(5)
